name: Raw milk for height

lead: Raw milk for height is the belief that unpasteurised milk helps people grow taller. Reference sources show dairy-rich diets track with taller populations but do not single out raw milk.
No study of raw milk and height was found.

paras: Believers point to the protein and nutrients in milk. Sources report heating does not substantially change nutritional value.

The CDC and FDA recommend against raw milk because it can carry pathogens such as Listeria, Salmonella and E. coli, with highest risk in young children, older adults, pregnancy and weakened immunity. Legal status varies by country and US state.

lead: Raw milk for height refers to the belief, circulating in some height-focused online circles under slogans such as Raw Milk + Healthy = Holy Height, that drinking unpasteurised milk promotes growth. Wikipedia defines raw milk as milk that has not been pasteurised and reports that proponents say it tastes better, is more nutritious and supports immunity.[1]

Wikipedia reports that the article finds no clear nutritional or health benefit, that the FDA says pasteurisation does not destroy nutritional value, and that the CDC and FDA strongly recommend against drinking raw milk because of pathogen risk.[1] Wikipedia's article on human height notes that populations eating more dairy and animal protein tend to be taller, without distinguishing raw from pasteurised milk.[2] The sources reviewed do not mention raw milk and height in children.
infobox: CDC and FDA advise against consumption[1]

paras: Wikipedia reports that average height correlates with protein quality, with populations eating more meat, dairy, eggs and fish tending to be taller than those relying on cereals.[2] It describes this as a population-level association and cites historical cases of cattle-rich regions with taller people.[2]

A 2013 review by Claeys and colleagues, as summarised on Wikipedia, found that most studies claiming protective effects of raw milk lacked objective confirmation of raw status or a comparison with heat-treated milk, and that apart from flavour heating does not substantially change nutritional value.[1] A 2012 Belgian federal review concluded raw milk poses a realistic health threat.[1]

Wikipedia lists pathogens that have been found in raw milk including Listeria, Salmonella, E. coli, Campylobacter, Brucella and Cryptosporidium, and says children under five, adults over 65, pregnant women and immunocompromised people are at highest risk, with complications including haemolytic-uraemic syndrome and death.[1] It reports 144 US raw-milk-linked outbreaks from 2007 to 2016, a federal ban on interstate sale for human consumption since 1987, state-by-state rules in the US, restricted farm sales in the UK and varied national rules in the EU.[1]
No studies found on raw milk and height.
